raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old man was admitted at a secondary-care hospital in the Brazilian Amazon with acute abdominal pain after jumping from a tree denying to have suffered any direct abdominal trauma. A diagnosis of spleen rupture and intra-abdominal haemorrhage was performed. He was submitted to splenectomy, during which a large spleen of 1,300 grams with a capsule rupture in the colic surface was obtained. The patient lived in an urban area of Manaus and denied previous episodes of malaria. For the last month before the traumatic event he had been working in a building project in a rural area where malaria transmission is endemic and referred that in the two days preceding surgery he had been feeling feverish and complaining of mild headache and asthenia. After surgery, he developed high fever, chills, and generalized myalgia. The initial diagnostic investigation performed by the Surgery Department only revealed anemia (Hb 8.7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (66,000 platelets/mm3). The patient was then transferred to a tertiary-care infectious diseases reference center.
A thick blood smear disclosed P. vivax infection with a semiquantitative parasitemia between 10.000 and 100.000 parasites/mm3. Real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from the peripheral blood confirmed P. vivax monoinfection. Treatment was initiated with chloroquine (1,500 mg divided in 3 days) and primaquine (30 mg/day during 7 days). Both fever and parasitemia were cleared within 48 hours. The patient was discharged in the third day of treatment, and he did not develop any relapse nor had any other complications through a 1-year follow-up.
The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Fundacao de Medicina Tropical Heitor Vieira Dourado and the National Committee of Ethics in Science and Technology (CONEP Process No.: 25.001.011.792/2009-15), and the patient consented his case to be published.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old man in the Brazilian Amazon presented with acute abdominal pain after jumping from a tree, preceded by 2 days of low-grade fever, mild headache, and asthenia, and followed post-splenectomy by high fever, chills, and generalized myalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: After working for 1 month on a rural building project in a malaria-endemic area near Manaus, the patient experienced 2 days of feverishness, mild headache, and asthenia before developing acute abdominal pain after jumping from a tree without direct abdominal blow. Following emergency splenectomy for splenic rupture, he developed high fever, chills, and generalized myalgia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Urban resident of Manaus with 1 month of recent occupational exposure in a rural malaria-endemic area; denied prior malaria episodes or direct abdominal trauma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute abdominal pain, fever, chills, mild headache, asthenia, and generalized myalgia.

objective.physical_examination: Presented with acute surgical abdomen from intra-abdominal hemorrhage and splenic rupture, followed postoperatively by high fever.
objective.routine_investigations: Post-splenectomy labs showed anemia (Hb 8.7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (66,000 platelets/mm3).
objective.advanced_workup: Surgical pathology of the resected spleen showed massive splenomegaly (1,300 g) with a capsular rupture on the colic surface.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Plasmodium vivax malaria complicated by atraumatic/indirect-trauma splenic rupture requiring splenectomy. Confirmed by thick blood smear showing P. vivax (10,000-100,000 parasites/mm3) and peripheral blood real-time PCR confirming P. vivax monoinfection. Treated with emergency splenectomy followed by oral chloroquine (1,500 mg over 3 days) and primaquine (30 mg/day for 7 days), clearing fever and parasitemia within 48 hours with no relapse over 1 year of follow-up.
